title: Shankara at his mother's side
hook: a boy in a crocodile's jaws makes his mother a promise, and keeps it years later at her bedside
carry: God beyond form, and God to love

segments.voice: Yesterday, svatantra: only God is independent, and tat tvam asi heard as you are his. Today, the last of these two weeks, and the teacher of not two at his mother's side.

A boy is bathing in a river in Kerala when a crocodile grabs his leg. His mother is on the bank. He calls to her: let me become a monk, now, and I can die a monk. Terrified, she says yes. The crocodile, the story says, lets go. The boy is Shankara, who will grow up to teach not two. Before he leaves home, he makes her a promise: when your time comes, wherever I am, I'll be there.
screen: `A CROCODILE IN THE RIVER.` → `LET ME BECOME A MONK.` → `I'LL BE THERE WHEN YOUR TIME COMES.`

segments.voice: Years later, the traditional lives of Shankara say, he feels her calling and comes home. She's dying. And the great teacher of not two does what he knows best: he speaks to her of Brahman beyond every form, no shape, no name, pure being. She can't hold it. She wants a God she can picture. So he sings to her instead, hymns to God with a form, and tradition says that as he sang to Vishnu, she died at peace. Here's the teaching. Hindus speak of Brahman in two ways: nirguna, without qualities, beyond every form, and saguna, with qualities, God with a face and a name you can love. Shankara's school says the formless is the final truth, and still honors worship of God with a face as real and good on the way. A short hymn credited to him, the Shatpadi, six verses, says it in one line, paraphrased: even when difference is gone, Lord, I am yours; you are not mine. The wave belongs to the ocean, never the ocean to the wave. Look at the map you've walked. Shankara: not two. Ramanuja: one, with the world as God's body. Madhva: two, forever. Chaitanya: one and different, beyond thought. The tradition kept them all. So one Hindu home can hold a father sitting in silence with not two, and a grandmother singing to Krishna. God beyond form, and God to love.
screen: `A PROMISE KEPT AT HER BEDSIDE.` · `NIRGUNA: BEYOND EVERY FORM.` · `SAGUNA: GOD WITH A FACE.` · `THE WAVE BELONGS TO THE OCEAN.` · then, large: `GOD BEYOND FORM, AND GOD TO LOVE.`

segments.voice: Two ways Hindus pray, side by side. First, with a name: say one name of God slowly a few times, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, Rama, whichever is yours, the way families do japa on a string of beads. Then let the name go, and sit in silence, no picture, no word, just being here. Go back and forth once or twice. If you don't pray, say a word that matters to you, then rest in the quiet after it.
Shatpadi, the six-verse hymn credited to Shankara: even when difference is gone, I am yours. Nirguna and saguna, God beyond form and God to love: the tradition keeps both.
Your line: God beyond form, and God to love. The wave is still a wave, and still the ocean's. Two weeks, done; see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus pray both ways: with a name and a form, through japa, puja and song to Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess or Rama, and in silent meditation on Brahman beyond form; the schools of Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva and Chaitanya are all still taught in monasteries and lineages today.

what a scholar hears: Advaita treats saguna Brahman (Ishvara) as real at the level of practice (vyavaharika) while nirguna Brahman is final (paramarthika); the deathbed story is from the Shankara Digvijaya hagiographies, and authorship of the hymns credited to Shankara is debated.

Chaitanya's school: achintya-bhedabheda, systematized by his followers (the Gosvamis); confirm the phrase 'one and different at the same time, in a way no mind can fully grasp'.
